questions.q: What is the term for the mathematical ratio (approx. 1:1.618) often used by Renaissance architects to achieve 'perfect' proportions?
questions.n: Renaissance architects believed this ratio reflected a universal, divine harmony found in both nature and geometry.

questions.q: Unlike the verticality of Gothic architecture, Renaissance facades emphasized what directional orientation?
questions.n: Renaissance design favored human-scaled stability, emphasized through horizontal string courses, cornices, and entablatures.

questions.q: What is the term for a roofed gallery or open porch, often supported by columns, which was a common feature of Renaissance villas and palaces?
questions.n: A loggia acts as a transitional space between the interior and the exterior, often facing an open courtyard or plaza.

questions.q: Renaissance architects replaced the 'pointed' arches of the Middle Ages with what classical form?
questions.n: The return to the semi-circular arch was a direct revival of Roman construction methods and aesthetics.

questions.q: What is Sgraffito, a decorative technique often used on Renaissance building exteriors?
questions.n: By scratching through a top layer of plaster to reveal a colored layer underneath, architects created durable, intricate patterns.

questions.q: Which building is the largest temple on the Peloponnese and served as the model for the Parthenon?
questions.n: This temple represented the pinnacle of the Doric order in its fully developed, classical form.

questions.q: What is the name of the circular building (tholos) in Athens that served as the dining hall for the Senate?
o: The Prytaneion (or Tholos of the Agora)
questions.n: This circular structure was the administrative heart where the executive committee of the Senate lived and dined.

questions.q: Which structure is known as the 'first' stadium to host the Panathenaic Games, originally built of timber and later marble?
questions.n: It is the only stadium in the world built entirely of marble and was restored for the first modern Olympics.

questions.q: The Choragic Monument of Lysicrates is famous for being the first external use of which Greek Order?
questions.n: Before this monument, the Corinthian order was primarily used for interior columns (e.g., Temple of Apollo at Bassae).

questions.q: What is the name of the 'altar' dedicated to Zeus, famous for its massive frieze depicting the Gigantomachy, now housed in a museum in Berlin?
questions.n: This Hellenistic masterpiece features an enormous 'U' shaped staircase surrounded by dramatic, high-relief sculptures.

questions.q: Sullivan divided the 'Tall Office Building' into three distinct parts based on a classical column. What are these three parts?
o: Base (Ground/Mezzanine), Shaft (Identical office floors), and Capital (The Attic/Cornice)
questions.n: By organizing the facade this way, Sullivan provided a logical visual order to the skyscraper's unprecedented height.

questions.q: In which building did Sullivan use the 'Transportation Curtains' and a massive golden arch as the main entrance?
questions.n: This massive mixed-use building showcased Sullivan's early mastery of acoustic design and ornate detail.

questions.q: What is the name of the department store in Chicago (now Target) famous for Sullivan's intricate cast-iron 'organic' ornamentation at the corner entrance?
o: Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building
questions.n: The ornament at the base is so intricate it is often compared to lace or iron 'foliage'.

questions.q: Who was Louis Sullivan's most famous 'head draftsman,' whom he referred to as Lieber Meister (Dear Master)?
questions.n: Wright worked for Sullivan for seven years and was deeply influenced by his philosophy of organic design.

questions.q: Sullivan’s ornament was rarely classical; instead, he drew inspiration from what source?
questions.n: He believed that ornament should grow from the building's surface like a plant from its soil.

questions.q: What is the name of the central open courtyard in a Roman Domus, which contained the impluvium to collect rainwater?
questions.n: The atrium was the public heart of the home, where guests were received and water was managed.

questions.q: What was the name of the Roman multi-story apartment block where the lower-middle class lived?
questions.n: Insulae were the predecessors to modern apartment buildings, often reaching 5-7 stories in height.

questions.q: In a wealthy Roman house, what was the name of the private study or office where the master (paterfamilias) kept his records?
questions.n: Located between the atrium and the peristyle, this room acted as the master's base of operations.

questions.q: What do you call the colonnaded garden or open courtyard located at the rear of a Roman house, influenced by Greek design?
questions.n: This addition transformed the Roman house into a more luxurious, indoor-outdoor dwelling space.

questions.q: What was the Triclinium used for in a Roman home?
questions.n: Its name refers to the 'three couches' arranged in a 'U' shape around a central table.

questions.q: During the Paleolithic (Stone Age) period, what was the primary climatic driver that led humans to seek shelter in caves or mammoth-bone huts?
questions.n: Severe temperatures forced early humans to prioritize thermal protection and portable, heavy-duty structures.

questions.q: In Ancient Mesopotamia, the hot, dry climate and lack of timber/stone led to the widespread use of what primary building material?
questions.n: Mud was plentiful in the river valleys and provided excellent insulation against the desert sun.

questions.q: How did the Ancient Egyptians utilize the 'thermal mass' of their temple walls to deal with the intense desert heat?
questions.n: The mass of the stone absorbed solar heat during the day, keeping the interior cool, and released it slowly at night.

questions.q: In the Ancient Greek climate, what architectural feature was developed to provide shaded outdoor circulation protected from the midday sun?
questions.n: The stoa allowed for public life, commerce, and philosophy to occur in a shaded, ventilated environment.

questions.q: What is the term for the 'wind-catcher' or ventilation shaft used in ancient Middle Eastern climates to pull cool air into the building?
questions.n: These towers catch prevailing winds and direct them downward into the living spaces, sometimes over water for cooling.
